p138.002: On the afternoon of the day he preached about the kingdom, Jesus called his six apostles together and talked about his plan to visit the cities around the Sea of Galilee. He did not invite his brothers James and Jude to this meeting, because he had decided not to include his close family in the apostolic group. Because of this the distance between Jesus and his family slowly grew, and this gap was not fully closed until after his death and resurrection. His mother Mary swung back and forth between faith and disappointment, but Ruth, the youngest, never once lost her faith in her brother.
p138.004: Jesus sent the six apostles out two by two. He told them not to baptize or preach in public, but to meet people one at a time and share the good news. He also told them that he would soon set up twelve apostles, so each of them should choose one person from among the believers. The apostles were a little disappointed and afraid, but Andrew encouraged them, saying that the Master “⟦Q 138:1.3⟧has manifested great confidence in us inasmuch as he has intrusted us with the choosing of these six new apostles⟦/Q⟧”.
p138.005: Meanwhile Jesus visited his family in Nazareth and did everything he could to keep their love and trust. He also longed to rescue John, who was in prison, but once again he waited for the Father's will.
p138.007: The first two-week trip was a great success. The apostles learned how precious it is to meet people personally, and that religion is, in the end, a personal experience. When they came back, each recommended one person, and with everyone's approval six new men were chosen.
p138.008: They were Matthew Levi, a tax collector; Thomas, a fisherman and carpenter; the twin brothers James and Judas Alpheus, who were fishermen; Simon, a leader among the Zealots who resisted Rome; and Judas Iscariot, who came from a wealthy family and had experience handling money. Judas Iscariot was the only one of the twelve apostles from Judea.
p138.009: 3. The Call of Matthew and Simon
p138.010: Jesus said to Matthew, who was sitting at the tax office, “⟦Q 138:3.1⟧Follow me⟦/Q⟧”, and Matthew got up and followed him. Then Simon received the same call. That evening Matthew gave a banquet for his family and friends, and many of the guests were people the Pharisees called “⟦Q 138:3.4⟧publicans and sinners⟦/Q⟧”. In those days it was the custom for people to stand around and watch such banquets, so the Pharisees came and watched too.
p138.011: When one Pharisee criticized him for eating and celebrating with such people, Jesus answered, “⟦Q 138:3.6⟧they who are whole need not a physician, but rather those who are sick⟦/Q⟧”. He had come to call not the righteous but sinners. As the people went home, they talked about Jesus' goodness and kindness.
p138.013: The next day at Kheresa, Jesus called the twin brothers James and Judas Alpheus. And he taught, “⟦Q 138:4.2⟧All men are my brothers⟦/Q⟧”. Because the heavenly Father looks down on no one, they should never refuse to eat with anyone, whether Pharisee or sinner, rich or poor, free or slave. The doors of the kingdom of heaven are wide open to everyone who seeks God.
p138.014: 5. The Call of Thomas and Judas
p138.015: At Tarichea, Jesus called Thomas, saying, “⟦Q 138:5.1⟧Thomas, you lack faith; nevertheless, I receive you⟦/Q⟧”. He called Judas Iscariot, telling him that he prayed Judas would always be loyal to his Galilean brothers. In this way the twelve apostles were gathered.
p138.016: Jesus taught them about the work of the Holy Spirit and the angels, but because the apostles tried to fit the new teaching into the ideas they already had, they did not understand much of it. Jesus also had them spend a day on their own so they could get to know one another. And he told them not to clash with the government, and to leave the rebuking of rulers to him.
p138.018: The next week was a time of intensive training. Each of the first six apostles taught the new apostle he had recommended everything he had learned so far, and in the evenings they all gathered to hear Jesus teach. Jesus set aside every Wednesday as a day off and would often say, “⟦Q 138:6.2⟧My children, go for a day of play⟦/Q⟧”. He knew that rest and play are truly necessary for people.
p138.019: Jesus told the apostles to proclaim not stories about himself, but the gospel of the kingdom of heaven and the heavenly Father. And he always urged them, “⟦Q 138:6.4⟧Go seek for the sinners; find the downhearted and comfort the anxious⟦/Q⟧”. Jesus had tremendous power, yet he wanted to do the Father's work in the quietest and least showy way.
p138.021: One day Peter, James, and Judas Iscariot came to Jesus and asked when the kingdom would be set up and what positions each of them would have then. Jesus asked, “⟦Q 138:7.1⟧Have I not made it plain to you that my kingdom is not of this world?⟦/Q⟧” and told them to give up the idea of a kingdom of power and glory. The apostles were shocked, but after praying together they promised to stay loyal to the end even if they did not understand it all.
p138.022: When Jesus learned that the apostles did not even have enough money to last two weeks, he suggested that they spend two weeks fishing to earn money and two weeks going out to meet people. Then he said, “⟦Q 138:7.6⟧And then will you go forth to become fishers of men⟦/Q⟧”. Jesus was a fine fisherman and a cheerful companion. Matthew said of him, “⟦Q 138:7.6⟧even the less I comprehend him, the more I love him⟦/Q⟧”.
p138.024: The apostles went out two by two, and Jesus took turns going with each pair. Jesus taught that sins are forgiven through faith in God, without self-punishment or sacrifices, and that the heavenly Father loves all his children with the same eternal love. John had said to repent in order to escape the coming wrath, but Jesus taught that faith is the open door into God's love.
p138.025: The apostles were moved by how deeply Jesus respected everyone he met. Even in the middle of an important conversation, he would go over to a woman carrying a heavy load and speak kindly to her, or he would play with a child who came up to him. To Jesus, the one person right in front of him was the most important. Jesus also clearly taught that in the kingdom of heaven women enjoy rights equal to men's.
p138.027: The five months of taking turns between fishing and ministry were a hard test for the apostles, but they held on to the end. During this time, living close to Jesus, the apostles came to think of him as their best friend in the world. The Urantia Book says that what held the apostles together later, in the dark hours of the cross, was not his wonderful teaching or miracles, but this very friendship and loyalty.
p138.028: Meanwhile almost all of Jesus' family except Ruth turned away from him, and they nearly came to think he was out of his mind. During this time the apostles also arranged to provide for their families, so that they could give themselves to the Master's work without worry.
p138.030: The apostles divided up the duties among themselves. Andrew became the chairman who led the whole group, and Peter, James, and John became the personal companions who stayed by Jesus' side. Philip was the steward who provided food, Nathaniel looked after the needs of the apostles' families, Matthew managed the finances, and Thomas arranged the travel and lodging.
p138.031: The Alpheus twins kept order among the crowds, Simon took care of the Wednesday rest and play, and Judas Iscariot kept the money bag. Having finished these preparations, the apostles were officially ordained the following January as ambassadors of the kingdom of heaven. Just as these men, once ordinary fishermen and tax collectors, became a team by sharing out their roles, we too can accomplish great things together when each of us faithfully does the work given to us in our own place.
p139.002: Jesus shattered the apostles' dreams of getting ahead many times. Even so, only one of them ever abandoned him. This shows how attractive and upright Jesus' life was. The apostles learned about the kingdom of heaven from Jesus, and Jesus learned a great deal about human nature from them. The twelve men each had a different personality. And they were not uneducated, as people often think. Except for the Alpheus twins, all of them had finished the synagogue schools; they simply had not received the higher education of the rabbis.
p139.004: Andrew was the first apostle chosen and the leader of the apostolic group. At thirty-three he was the oldest of the twelve, and the most able. He was not a good preacher, but he was excellent at sharing the gospel with people one by one, and he brought his brother Simon Peter to Jesus. Even when his brother became more famous, he was not jealous at all. When two thousand people came to believe through Peter's preaching at Pentecost, Andrew said, “⟦Q 139:1.6⟧I could not do that, but I am glad I have a brother who could⟦/Q⟧”.
p139.005: Andrew had the sharpest eye of all for judging people, and he was the first to notice that something was going wrong in Judas' heart. He was calm and dependable, but his weakness was that he was slow to praise his fellows. He admired Jesus' steady sincerity. Later, while preaching the gospel in many lands, he was crucified, and even while hanging there for two days he kept proclaiming the good news.
p139.007: Simon Peter was impulsive and optimistic. His words often ran ahead of his thinking and got him into trouble, but he was a good speaker and a natural leader of people. He asked more questions than anyone, and he acted so quickly that when he saw the risen Jesus he jumped into the water and swam to him. He took deeply to heart Jesus' gentleness, especially the teaching to forgive “⟦Q 139:2.5⟧not only seven times but seventy times and seven⟦/Q⟧”.
p139.008: Peter was brave when attacked head-on, but he shrank back when he was mocked. That is why, at a servant girl's words, he ended up denying his Lord. But after he knew he had been forgiven, the fire of the kingdom burned brightly in his heart, and he became the greatest preacher of the twelve. His wife also worked faithfully alongside him. Peter ended his life in Rome, counting it an honor to die on a cross like his Lord.
p139.010: James was the older of Zebedee's two sons, and Jesus called him and his brother John the “⟦Q 139:3.1⟧sons of thunder⟦/Q⟧”. When he got angry, he flared up like fire, and he also had the weakness of going silent for days. But he could see the many sides of any problem, and of the twelve he understood the real meaning of Jesus' teaching best. He admired Jesus' warm love, which made no difference between great and small, rich and poor.
p139.011: James was a humble worker and a good balance for Peter. He was the first of the apostles to be martyred, by the sword of Herod Agrippa. He carried himself with such dignity to the very last moment that even the man who had accused him was moved and became a disciple of Jesus.
p139.013: John was the youngest apostle, twenty-four years old, and he was a trustworthy man who took care of the affairs of Jesus' family. With Peter and James, he became one of the three personal aides who helped Jesus at his side. The Urantia Book says it is hard to say that Jesus loved one apostle more than the others. John had a hidden conceit and a narrow mind, but he changed greatly by living with Jesus.
p139.014: John was deeply moved by Jesus' love and unselfishness. So this “⟦Q 139:4.6⟧son of thunder⟦/Q⟧” at last became the “⟦Q 139:4.6⟧apostle of love⟦/Q⟧”. When he was old and no longer had the strength to preach, he kept repeating only, “⟦Q 139:4.6⟧My little children, love one another.⟦/Q⟧” He was the only apostle who followed Jesus all the way on the night he was arrested, and he was the first to fully believe in the resurrection. Later he was exiled to the island of Patmos, then looked after the churches at Ephesus, and he died peacefully at the age of one hundred and one.
p139.016: Philip was the fifth apostle, and he served as the steward who provided supplies. He lacked imagination, but he was careful and methodical, so for four years they almost never ran out of food. He was always asking “⟦Q 139:5.5⟧be shown⟦/Q⟧”, and he would ask odd questions even in the middle of Jesus' deepest talks. But Jesus never once scolded him. He knew that if he did, this honest man would never again feel free to ask. Philip looked up to Jesus' unfailing generosity.
p139.017: Philip had a rare gift for saying “⟦Q 139:5.8⟧Come⟦/Q⟧”. When Nathaniel doubted, he simply said, “⟦Q 139:5.8⟧Come and see⟦/Q⟧”. The Urantia Book says that even parents can learn from Philip to say to their children not “⟦Q 139:5.8⟧Go do this⟦/Q⟧”, but “⟦Q 139:5.8⟧Come with us⟦/Q⟧”. Philip was the first to bring the gospel to people who were not Jews, and later he was crucified for his faith.
p139.019: Nathaniel was an honest man with no deceit in him. His weakness was pride, and he said, “⟦Q 139:6.3⟧Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?⟦/Q⟧” But the moment he saw Jesus' face, he changed his mind. He was the philosopher of the group and its funniest storyteller, and when tension arose among the apostles, he eased it with humor.
p139.020: When Judas secretly complained that Nathaniel was too lighthearted, Jesus corrected Judas, saying that it is not the Father's will for his children to enjoy only serious things. Nathaniel took charge of caring for the apostles' families, and he admired Jesus' broad-mindedness and tolerance most of all. Later he preached the gospel in Mesopotamia and India, and he died in India.
p139.022: Matthew Levi was a customs officer in Capernaum. He was deeply grateful that a tax collector, a man people despised, had been accepted, and he gave himself to the work with all his heart. He was in charge of raising money for the apostolic group, and although he gave almost all his own wealth, he gave it in other people's names so that no one knew. Even when his fellows looked down on tax collectors, he never revealed it.
p139.023: Matthew was most deeply grateful for Jesus' forgiving nature. Just by his being an apostle, the door of the kingdom swung wide open for many people who felt like outcasts. The sayings of Jesus that he wrote down later became the basis of the Gospel of Matthew. He preached the gospel in many regions and was put to death in Thrace.
p139.025: Later generations call Thomas “⟦Q 139:8.1⟧doubting Thomas⟦/Q⟧”, but his fellow apostles did not see him that way. He was the only one of the twelve with an analytical mind, the real scientist of the group. Because of an unhappy childhood he was pessimistic and hard to get along with, but the better you knew him, the more you found him to be completely honest and loyal. He marveled that Jesus' character perfectly combined love and justice, strength and gentleness.
p139.026: In meetings Thomas always argued for caution, but once a decision was made, he was the first to shout, “⟦Q 139:8.11⟧Let's go!⟦/Q⟧” Even when Jesus went to dangerous places, Thomas rallied the others, saying, “⟦Q 139:8.8⟧let's go and die with him⟦/Q⟧”. When he was depressed he sometimes went off by himself, but he learned that the harder things got, the better it was to work together with his fellows.
p139.027: The Urantia Book calls Thomas a fine example of a man who had doubts, faced them, and won. If there had been even a little deception, a man like Thomas would not have stayed to the end. He preached the gospel on many islands and in North Africa, and he was executed in Malta.
p139.029: James and Judas, the Alpheus twins, were ordinary fishermen. They did not understand the difficult discussions very well, but they loved Jesus, and Jesus loved them. They gladly guided the crowds and ran all kinds of errands. They were happy to think of themselves as “⟦Q 139:9.5⟧the least of all the apostles⟦/Q⟧”. Ordinary people took great courage when they saw that these twins, who were so much like themselves, had become apostles.
p139.030: The Urantia Book says that Jesus did not look down on small things; he looked down only on evil and sin. The twins stayed loyal to the end and believed in the resurrection early, but after the crucifixion they went back to their families and their nets. Still, all their lives they treasured the blessing of having spent four years with the Son of God.
p139.032: Simon the Zealot was a fiery agitator who had given his whole heart to the Zealots, who wanted to win back their nation. He was in charge of the apostles' play and rest, and he had such enthusiasm that he could lead a hesitating person to faith in fifteen minutes. He admired Jesus' calm, unshakable poise.
p139.033: Jesus often said that it is right to want society to get better, but that this is not the work of the kingdom of heaven. Simon did not easily get free of his nationalism, but little by little he became a preacher of “⟦Q 139:11.6⟧Peace on earth and good will among men⟦/Q⟧”. After the persecution he fell into despair for a while, but he rose again and carried the gospel deep into Africa.
p139.035: Judas Iscariot was the only one of the twelve apostles from Judea, and the best educated. He was in charge of the treasury and did the work honestly and capably; money was never his motive for betrayal. But because he had grown up pampered as an only son, he thought too highly of himself, could not stand losing, and had the habit of brooding over hurt feelings and seeking revenge.
p139.036: Jesus knew Judas' weaknesses from the beginning, but he accepted him in order to give every person the same chance. The Urantia Book says that when we receive light but do not live by it, it easily turns into darkness in the soul. Judas grew in his mind but not in his spirit, and his hurt feelings turned into resentment. When he was publicly rebuked over the woman who poured perfume on Jesus' feet, he at last betrayed his Lord.
p139.037: After it was all over, Judas took his own life. Jesus felt only pity for him. The story of the twelve apostles shows that people with many weaknesses, like us, can be changed by being with Jesus. At the same time it quietly warns us how dangerous it is to keep brooding over small hurts for a long time.
p140.002: On a Sunday in January of A.D. 27, Jesus called the twelve apostles together to set them apart as preachers of the gospel of the kingdom. Walking along the shore, he called Andrew and Peter, then James and John, and gathered the rest two by two. Then he went up into the hills north of Capernaum. Even Peter, who usually talked a lot, was quiet and thoughtful that day. The moment they had waited for so long had finally come.
p140.004: First Jesus explained what the kingdom of heaven is. The Father's kingdom is set up not by the power of armies or wealth, but by the spirit of God ruling people's hearts. God is not the God of the Jews only, nor of the gentiles only. We enter this kingdom by faith, but to keep growing we must bear the fruits of the spirit. That is why the one who enters is not “⟦Q 140:1.4⟧every one who says, 'Lord, Lord,'⟦/Q⟧” but the one who does the Father's will.
p140.005: Jesus said that the kingdom does not come in a way that lets people say “⟦Q 140:1.5⟧'it is here' or 'it is there,'⟦/Q⟧” because it is God within us. Whoever wants to be great must serve everyone. This small group, which began with twelve ordinary men, would grow until it filled the whole earth, and people would know that the apostles had been with Jesus not so much from their words as from their lives.
p140.007: Jesus had the apostles kneel in a circle, and one by one, from Judas Iscariot to Andrew, he laid his hands on their heads and blessed them. Then he prayed to the Father. He asked the Father to love these men as he loved him, and to give wisdom to those he would trust with the work of the coming kingdom. When the prayer was over, the apostles embraced Jesus one by one. No one spoke, and a deep silence settled over the place.
p140.009: Jesus said that now that the apostles had become ambassadors of the kingdom of heaven, they must live better lives than before. Then he gave them words to bring to people who were suffering: “⟦Q 140:3.6⟧Happy are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.⟦/Q⟧” In the same way, he said, happy are the humble, those who hunger for righteousness, the meek, those who mourn, the merciful, the peacemakers, and the persecuted.
p140.010: He also told the apostles that they were the salt and the light of the world. He told them not to resist injustice with violence, but to love their enemies and do good to those who hate them. He told them not to judge people but to save them, and to look first at the beam in their own eye before the speck in someone else's. He said that false prophets can be known by their fruits, and that God sees a person's inner heart and motives. The apostles had never before heard Jesus speak with such great authority.
p140.011: 4. You Are the Salt of the Earth
p140.012: These words, often called the “⟦Q 140:4.1⟧Sermon on the Mount⟦/Q⟧”, are not the whole gospel of Jesus; they are the charge he gave when he ordained the twelve apostles. In ancient times salt was so precious that it was used like money. Salt does its job by making other things taste good. Light drives away darkness, but it should not shine to draw attention to itself.
p140.013: The Urantia Book says that strong character comes not from simply not doing wrong, but from actually doing right. Happy people are moved not by fear of making mistakes but by love of doing what is right. Morality does not grow from prohibitions like “⟦Q 140:4.7⟧Thou shalt not⟦/Q⟧” alone, and fear and shame are not the right motives for faith. We cannot change our inborn urges, but we can change how we respond to them, so character can always grow.
p140.015: Jesus taught a fatherly love, loving people as Jesus loves us, which goes beyond the brotherly love of loving our neighbor as ourselves. People who are humble, thirsty for righteousness, meek, and pure in heart can come close to this kind of love. Meekness is not fear; it is the attitude of working together with God, saying, “⟦Q 140:5.11⟧Your will be done⟦/Q⟧”. A pure heart has no suspicion or desire for revenge, and it always looks for the best in people.
p140.016: The saying that those who mourn are blessed refers to a tender heart. The Urantia Book says it is a great mistake to teach boys that showing pain or feelings is unmanly. Mercy is the depth of true friendship, and the peace of Jesus is not just quietness but an active peace that guards us against fear and anger. A courageous young person does not run away from difficulties.
p140.017: So these blessed sayings rest not on law or duty but on faith and love. Fatherly love delights in returning good for evil.
p140.019: That evening, because the apostles did not understand Jesus' words well, they asked him to teach them more. Jesus told them not to try to force the new teaching on top of their old ideas, but to start over like little children. He said he had come not to destroy the law but to fulfill it. He said that God sees not only outward actions but also the intentions of the heart, and when they asked questions about things like divorce, he answered that he had not come to make laws but to enlighten souls.
p140.020: When Nathaniel asked about “⟦Q 140:6.9⟧An eye for an eye⟦/Q⟧”, Jesus told them to repay evil with good. When Jesus said that if these words were too hard they could still turn back, Peter answered that none of them would turn back. Jesus told them to do their good deeds in secret, not to worry too much about what they would eat and wear, and to seek first the kingdom of God. That night the apostles each talked with Jesus privately, one by one. When someone asked whether to wake the twins, who had fallen asleep by the fire, Jesus smiled and said to let them be.
p140.022: When the apostles said they did not feel quite ready yet and asked to stay a few more days, Jesus agreed. During that week the apostles themselves taught the people who came from many places. Jesus repeated the two purposes of his mission: to show the Father to people, and to lead people to realize by faith that they are children of God. The apostles did not understand all his teaching, but they did not miss the meaning of the beautiful life Jesus lived with them.
p140.024: On Thursday afternoon Jesus took Peter, James, and John out in a boat and talked with them about the kingdom for four hours. He said that trusting the Father does not mean sitting still and waiting, and that it is good to plan ahead but not to worry. Revenge is never right, but he accepted that the state may punish crime to keep order. He also told them not to identify his teaching with any political theory or economic system.
p140.025: Jesus taught a kindness that treats everyone as a neighbor, but he also said that careless kindness can actually do harm. He honored the family as the most precious human duty, and he warned not against wealth itself but against the effect wealth has on a person's heart. It was on this day that he first said “⟦Q 140:8.18⟧it is more blessed to give than to receive⟦/Q⟧”.
p140.026: The Urantia Book says that Jesus' teaching must be understood through his life. Jesus was a real man who knew the ways of the world, and “⟦Q 140:8.20⟧Fear not⟦/Q⟧” was his watchword. He taught true goodness rather than exposing evil, and he did not force people into one mold but let each grow in his own way. Jesus came to create in people a new spirit and a new will that know truth and choose the good.
p140.028: The next Sabbath, Jesus took the apostles back to the hill where he had ordained them and solemnly committed them to the Father. He called each one by name and charged them, “⟦Q 140:9.2⟧Freely you have received, freely give.⟦/Q⟧” He also told them that, like sheep sent among wolves, they should be wise as serpents and harmless as doves. They would meet hatred and persecution, but he told them not to be afraid, and promised that the Father's spirit would speak through them.
p140.030: That evening Jesus spoke at length not so much about what the apostles should do as about what kind of people they should be. The apostles knew only a religion of becoming righteous by doing good deeds, but Jesus said that we must first become righteous by faith, and then we can do those deeds. The apostles kept trying to turn his teaching into rigid rules, but by living with Jesus they gradually learned its spirit.
p140.031: When Thomas asked how being like a little child fits with not being fooled, Jesus said that being like a little child does not mean being easily fooled; it means the relationship of a child who trusts and loves his father. When Simon asked whether all people are sons of God, Jesus answered, “⟦Q 140:10.7⟧Yes, Simon, all men are the sons of God⟦/Q⟧”. The kingdom of heaven means recognizing God's rule, believing that we are his children, and believing in the desire to become like him. When we too think first about what kind of person we are becoming rather than what we are doing, we will come a step closer to the meaning of these words.
p141.002: In January of A.D. 27, Jesus and the twelve apostles got ready to leave Bethsaida to go to the Passover in Jerusalem. The apostles' families and disciples gathered to see them off. But just before they left, Jesus could not be found. When Andrew went looking, he found Jesus sitting in a boat by the shore, weeping. Jesus said he was sad not because of the apostles, but because no one from his own family had come to say goodbye. His family had stayed away because of pride, disappointment, and misunderstanding.
p141.004: As Jesus' name became widely known, he knew that Herod would soon take an interest in him, so he went south. The group stayed for more than two weeks by the Jordan near Pella, where Jesus had been baptized a year before. Hundreds of people gathered from many regions. Jesus did not preach himself but left that to the apostles, and in the evenings he talked with them.
p141.005: Many of those who gathered were disciples of John the Baptist. They could not understand why Jesus had not rescued John from prison. Andrew carefully taught the apostles how to get along well with John's disciples. More than three quarters of Jesus' followers in the first year had originally followed John.
p141.006: 2. God’s Law and the Father’s Will
p141.007: On the night before they left Pella, Jesus said that the kingdom of heaven is recognizing and acknowledging the rule of God in people's hearts. The king of this kingdom is our Father, and we are not only his people but his children. The Father rules the hearts of his children through the spirit he has sent to live within them.
p141.008: Jesus said this: when the Father's will is just a law you have to keep, you have barely entered the kingdom, but when the Father's will truly becomes your own will, the kingdom is realized within you. Then we are no longer slaves bound by law but free children of God. Only James fully understood what this meant, but these words stayed deep in the apostles' hearts.
p141.010: The group stayed near Amathus for almost three weeks. Peter, James, and John did most of the preaching, and the other apostles divided up the work of personal counseling, study groups, keeping order, and managing the household. Andrew was busy settling quarrels between John's disciples and the new disciples. Jesus did not step into these matters; he only said, “⟦Q 141:3.3⟧a wise parent never takes sides in the petty quarrels of his own children⟦/Q⟧”.
p141.011: The Urantia Book stresses that Jesus had a strong and forceful personality. He had a brilliant mind and unshakable poise, and at the same time he was patient, gentle, and humble. The Urantia Book says that pictures showing Jesus only as weak and frail have had a bad influence on young people. He was a man of dignity, and he did not just mean well; he actually did good.
p141.012: Jesus said he would give rest and strength not to the lazy but to those who labor. And when he said, “⟦Q 141:3.8⟧Resist not evil⟦/Q⟧”, he did not mean that we should overlook sin. He meant that we should not take revenge for insults and hurts done to us, but forgive them.
p141.014: At Amathus, Jesus taught a new idea of God: God is not a bookkeeper who writes down people's sins to judge them later, but a Father who loves each person one by one. When Thomas asked who the God of this kingdom is, Jesus answered that God is our Father, and that the gospel is coming to realize by faith the truth that we are his children.
p141.015: Jesus also taught them to see and care for a person as a being in whom body, mind, and spirit are united. He had them tell the difference between sickness of the body, troubles of the mind, and cases of possession by evil spirits. And he said that after the spirit was poured out on all people, evil spirits would no longer be able to torment them. During this year the apostles gave more and more of their effort to caring for the sick.
p141.017: When James asked how they could all come to think alike so they would get along better, Jesus asked him back when he had ever taught that they must all think alike. Jesus came to give spiritual freedom, so that people could live free and unique lives before God. What is needed is not sameness of thought but spiritual unity: all having the same motive of doing the Father's will, and heading toward the same goal of finding the Father and becoming like him.
p141.018: Even when our thoughts, personalities, and actions differ, we can be deeply united because of the same spirit of God living within each of us. That is why Jesus warned again and again not to force believers into the mold of one interpretation or one creed.
p141.020: Simon the Zealot could not persuade Teherma, a Persian he thought was a fire worshiper, but Teherma soon listened to Jesus' words. Jesus told Simon not to try to take anything away from the heart of someone seeking truth, but simply to feed the hungry soul. If you lead people into the kingdom, the living truth will drive out wrong ideas by itself. In the end Teherma also entered the kingdom.
p141.021: That night Jesus said that entering the kingdom is being born again. He told them to introduce people to God first, not to argue, and always to be patient. The kingdom did not belong to the apostles; they were only ambassadors, so all they had to do was share the good news that God is our Father and we are his children.
p141.023: At the end of February, the group moved to the ford near Bethany, where John had first proclaimed the kingdom, and stayed four weeks. Jesus took Peter, James, and John into the hills for three days and taught them many things. He said that believers should show the kingdom by their lives so that people would ask about it on their own. The only task of a gospel teacher, he said, is to show a person God as Father and help him realize that he is a child of God.
p141.024: Jesus stressed two truths as the most important: that salvation is gained by faith, and “⟦Q 141:7.6⟧You shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.⟦/Q⟧” He began his work not with people of high rank but with the poor, and he came to set an example of living for all people on all worlds. Jesus was more a teacher than a preacher, and he spoke directly to people's souls.
p141.025: The apostles came to see that Jesus was not swayed by praise or public opinion, that he never became angry or flustered, and that though he was sometimes sad, he was never discouraged. John realized more clearly that Jesus, as a real man, understood and loved people.
p141.027: While they were staying at Bethany, Andrew sent the apostles two by two to Jericho. In Jericho the apostles went from house to house comforting the sick. They found that the good news of the kingdom was a great comfort to sick people. In this way Jesus' command to preach the gospel and care for those who suffer was carried out fully for the first time in Jericho. Also, truth seekers from Mesopotamia spent three days with Jesus and went home happy.
p141.029: On the last day of March, Jesus and the apostles set out for Jerusalem. Lazarus offered his home in Bethany as a place for them to stay, and Martha and Mary warmly welcomed the Master and the apostles. After resting five days, on Sunday, April 6, Jesus and the twelve apostles entered Jerusalem together for the first time. This paper teaches that even if we do not all think alike, we can walk together toward the same Father, and that is a warm guide for us too, as different as we and our friends may be.
p142.002: During the month of April, Jesus and the apostles worked in Jerusalem by day and went out to Bethany to rest at night. Jesus sometimes stayed at the home of Flavius, a Greek Jew, where well-known Jews would come secretly to see him. On the first day Jesus visited his old friend Annas, the former high priest, but Annas greeted him coldly. As he left, Jesus said that fear holds people in bondage and pride is a great weakness, and he asked Annas whether he would become a slave to these two, which rob us of joy and freedom. Annas did not answer.
p142.004: All that month, either Jesus or one of the apostles taught in the temple every day. Their message was this: The kingdom of heaven is at hand. If you believe in God as your Father, you enter the kingdom and become a child of God. Loving God with all your heart and loving your neighbor as yourself is the rule of living in the kingdom. Following the Father's will and bearing the fruits of the spirit in your life is the law of the kingdom.
p142.005: Hundreds of people heard this good news and rejoiced, but the Jewish leaders worried about what to do with Jesus. The people who had gathered for the Passover carried the news to far parts of the Roman Empire and to the East. In this way the gospel began to spread beyond Palestine into the world.
p142.007: Jacob, a wealthy merchant from Crete, came to see Jesus secretly. He asked why the ancient prophets had taught that God is wrathful and vengeful, while Jesus taught that he is a loving Father. Jesus answered that God does not change, but people's understanding of him had grown wider and deeper from the time of Moses to the time of Isaiah.
p142.008: Then, since Jacob had six children, Jesus gave him this comparison. A young child who sees his father's scolding thinks only that his father is angry. But when he grows up, he should understand the love inside that scolding. As mankind grows up, it too should understand God more deeply. A good father truly loves not only his family as a whole but each child individually. Jacob answered, “⟦Q 142:2.5⟧Rabbi, I believe⟦/Q⟧”.
p142.010: That night, when the apostles asked many questions about God, Jesus explained how the Jewish people's idea of God had grown. It went from Yahweh, the god of the Sinai tribes, to the Most High that Melchizedek taught Abraham, to El Shaddai learned in Egypt, to Elohim, which calls to mind the Trinity, to the all-powerful and merciful Creator of Isaiah's time, and now to the Father in heaven. And he said that God never refuses sincere worship, whatever name people call him by.
p142.011: Jesus said that this change can be seen even within the Scriptures. An older record said that a certain event happened because of the Lord's anger, but a later record did not blame God for the evil and wrote that it was because of Satan. The commandments also grew, from old rules about sacrifices and feasts, to the new commandments of Sinai, and then to the law of love: love God, and love your neighbor as yourself. Jesus said that this law of love is the whole duty of man.
p142.013: Flavius loved paintings and sculpture so much that he had decorated his house with beautiful works of art. He was worried that Jesus would dislike these statues and call them idols. But Jesus looked at each work with admiration and asked many questions.
p142.014: Jesus said that it is not wrong to appreciate the beauty of what God has made and what human hands have shaped. Moses' ban on images was right for his time, to prevent idol worship. Now that the Father had been revealed through the Son, people could enjoy art without confusing it with the worship of God. In the coming kingdom, he said, they would no longer teach “⟦Q 142:4.2⟧Do not worship this and do not worship that⟦/Q⟧”; instead, truly worshiping God and lovingly serving one's neighbor would be at the center. Flavius believed and was baptized.
p142.016: In the temple a man from Damascus asked how he could know for sure that Jesus was sent by God and that he himself could enter the kingdom. Jesus answered that a good father would not leave his children anxious about whether he loved them. The heavenly Father does not leave his children of faith in doubt either.
p142.017: When we accept God as our Father, we truly are children of God, and God's spirit bears witness to this together with our spirit. Faith is the power that overcomes every uncertainty. Jesus said that the proof of being born of the spirit is sincerely loving one another. This teaching gave the apostles great assurance too.
p142.019: One night Nicodemus, an elder of the Sanhedrin, the highest Jewish council, came to see Jesus, keeping out of sight of others. Jesus neither made a special fuss over him nor pushed him away, but treated him calmly and earnestly. Jesus said, “⟦Q 142:6.4⟧except a man be born from above, he cannot see the kingdom of God⟦/Q⟧”. When Nicodemus asked how an old man could be born again, Jesus said that being born of the spirit is like the wind: you cannot see it, but you can tell it is there by the sound of rustling leaves.
p142.020: When Nicodemus asked how he could lay hold of that spirit, Jesus said that the Father's spirit was already within him, and that if he sincerely chose to be led by that spirit and made doing the Father's will the purpose of his life, he would be born of the spirit. Nicodemus was a man of fine morals, but he did not know how to entrust his will to God like a little child. Still, his faith grew, and later, when the disciples had scattered, he and Joseph of Arimathea took Jesus' body for burial.
p142.022: After the Passover, Thomas asked how they should teach people to live. Jesus said that the kingdom is an experience that begins on this earth and grows all the way to Paradise. He also said that people of later times would understand the gospel better if it were explained not with the word ‘kingdom’ but in terms of family, saying that God is our Father and men are brothers.
p142.023: Jesus said that a true family rests on seven things: passing on life, giving security and pleasure, teaching and training, correcting when needed, always being there together, a love that forgives without holding a grudge, and providing for the future. Our relationship with the heavenly Father is like this too.
p142.024: When Thomas asked why, then, there is so much suffering and why prayers are not always answered, Jesus told them not to apply the family comparison too literally to material problems. The kingdom is a spiritual kingdom, and the Father is spirit. Even so, Jesus said he would love the apostles and be patient with them to the end.
p142.026: At the end of April, when opposition grew fierce, Jesus and the apostles went to Bethlehem and Hebron and spent the month of May going from house to house meeting people. Jesus also visited the Nazarite community at Engedi, where John the Baptist had grown up, but most of them would not accept Jesus because he did not teach fasting. In June they returned to Jerusalem, pitched their tents in the Garden of Gethsemane, and quietly taught the believers.
p142.027: Then, when Simon, a member of the Sanhedrin, openly took Jesus' side, there was a new move to arrest him, and Jesus withdrew to Samaria and the Decapolis. This paper invites us to know God not as a fearsome judge but as a Father who loves each of us one by one.
p143.002: At the end of June in A.D. 27, as the opposition of the Jewish leaders grew fierce, Jesus and the twelve apostles left Jerusalem and went north toward Samaria. For more than two weeks they taught both Jews and Samaritans in various villages. The apostles overcame much of their prejudice against the Samaritans, but Judas Iscariot alone found it hard to love them.
p143.004: In the first half of August, the group stayed in Archelais and Phasaelis, Greek cities near the Jordan. It was the apostles' first experience of preaching the gospel almost entirely to gentiles. Philip reported that the people there sneered that Jesus' teaching was fit only for weaklings and slaves and that it made people soft.
p143.005: Jesus answered with unusual feeling. He said that love is the greatest of all spiritual realities, and that someday this gospel would rule the world. He asked whether John, or they, or he himself looked weak, and he said that the gospel is for everyone: rich and poor, men and women, old and young. He also said that the road to Paradise is not a comfortable journey but the greatest of all adventures.
p143.006: The Urantia Book says that physical courage is the lowest kind of courage, courage of the mind is higher, and the highest courage is loyalty that holds on to deep spiritual truth to the end. It takes more courage to quietly give up your life alone out of love for truth than to die with your comrades beside you. After hearing these words, the apostles' preaching took on a new spirit of boldness and courage.
p143.008: Jesus was a perfect example of a man who ruled himself; when he was insulted, he did not insult in return. When Andrew asked whether they should live a life of self-denial like John's, Jesus said that if John's way was a religion of watching and holding down the self, he was teaching a new way of forgetting the self and mastering it. He said, “⟦Q 143:2.3⟧he who rules his own self is greater than he who captures a city⟦/Q⟧”.
p143.009: The old way was to hold yourself down while struggling to keep the rules. The new way is first to have your mind made new by the Spirit of Truth, and then by that power to do God's will gladly. Jesus said that when we do wrong it is easy to blame others, but very often we are being fooled by our own hearts. Salvation is a gift received by faith, and a person born of the spirit, instead of watching himself in fear, naturally bears the fruits of the spirit in his life. This is true self-mastery.
p143.011: By this time the apostles were very tired. They were still not good at living together, they often clashed with John's disciples, and meeting gentiles and Samaritans was hard for them. When Andrew asked for help, Jesus did not solve their problems for them. Instead he suggested that they all go up Mount Sartaba together and rest for three days, and that they not talk about their worries during that time.
p143.012: On the mountain Jesus told them to learn the value of rest and a change of pace. Getting away from tangled problems for a while is often the very best way to solve them. The apostles spent the day talking about things that had nothing to do with religion. When they came down the mountain, they realized that many of their worries had come from exaggerated fears. They looked at one another and laughed from the heart, and their relationship with John's disciples became much better too.
p143.014: The Jews and the Samaritans had been on bad terms with each other for more than six hundred years. The Urantia Book traces the reasons in history: Assyria carried off the people of northern Israel as captives and settled people from other lands there; the Samaritans hindered the Jews who returned from exile as they rebuilt Jerusalem; and the Samaritans built a temple of their own on Mount Gerizim. All these things piled up. So when Jesus said, “⟦Q 143:4.3⟧Let us go into Samaria⟦/Q⟧”, the apostles' loyalty was put to a severe test. But their faith in Jesus was greater than their prejudice.
p143.016: While resting by Jacob's well, Jesus asked Nalda, a Samaritan woman who had come to draw water, for a drink. In those days a Jewish man almost never spoke to a Samaritan woman, so she was startled. Jesus said that whoever drinks this water will be thirsty again, but whoever drinks the living water of the spirit will never be thirsty again.
p143.017: Nalda had a painful story. Her husband had unfairly cast her off, and in her hard situation she was living with another man without being married. At first she misunderstood Jesus' kindness, but when Jesus saw right into her situation, she was ashamed and repented. Even so, to avoid her own problem, she changed the subject with a question about where people should worship. Jesus answered, “⟦Q 143:5.6⟧God is spirit, and they who worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth⟦/Q⟧”.
p143.018: When she spoke of the coming Deliverer, Jesus said, “⟦Q 143:5.7⟧I who speak to you am he⟦/Q⟧”. This woman was the first person to whom Jesus clearly revealed who he was. The Urantia Book says that in God's eyes she was more a soul who had been wronged than one who had sinned, a soul longing for salvation. Nalda ran to the village and brought the people back. The Urantia Book says that the world should be more interested in Jesus' happy life, which showed God, than in his death.
p143.020: When the apostles urged him to eat, Jesus said, “⟦Q 143:6.1⟧My meat is to do the will of Him who sent me⟦/Q⟧”. Then, pointing to the Samaritans streaming toward them, he said that the time had come to harvest the seeds John the Baptist had sown. The apostles thought Jesus would scold them because of his talk with the woman, but Jesus said nothing about it.
p143.021: Instead, on Mount Gerizim he taught them to see God as Father and friend, and he stressed that love is the greatest relationship in the universe. The group stayed there until the end of August, preaching the gospel in many villages of Samaria. This work later became the foundation for the great harvest Philip gathered in Samaria.
p143.023: At the evening gatherings on Mount Gerizim, Jesus taught about prayer and worship. True religion is the relationship of an individual soul with God. Worship and service, work and play, faith and humor should all be in balance. Prayer widens our insight more than it adds to our knowledge, and it holds us steady spiritually.
p143.024: The Urantia Book says that if prayer is noble thinking that remembers the self, worship is thinking that forgets the self. Worship is true rest that takes no effort, and it is our finite selves keeping step with the infinite God. On the busiest and most tiring days especially, a moment of stopping to rest and look to God will give us new strength.
p144.002: In September and October, Jesus and the apostles lived quietly at an out-of-the-way camp on the slopes of Mount Gilboa. The opposition of the leaders in Jerusalem was strong, and Herod still had John the Baptist in prison and was suspicious about the connection between Jesus and John. Tension was also growing between John's disciples and Jesus' apostles. Jesus knew he would soon begin his last great work, but he hoped it would not cause John any distress.
p144.004: Jesus gave three reasons for staying there: to strengthen their understanding of and faith in the gospel, to wait for the opposition to die down, and to watch what would happen to John. The apostles rested and sorted out what they had learned so far. But they each had different ideas about whether the kingdom had already come or had not come yet.
p144.005: Jesus often went up the mountain alone to commune with the Father. The main topic of this period was prayer and worship. The apostles needed a prayer to teach the new believers. Jesus did not much like prayers in a fixed form, but he answered Thomas' request, “⟦Q 144:1.9⟧Master, teach us how to pray⟦/Q⟧”.
p144.007: Jesus said that prayer is the heart of the soul turning toward God of its own accord, and that “⟦Q 144:2.3⟧Prayer is the breath of the soul⟦/Q⟧”. Even a man who goes to borrow bread from a friend at midnight will get it in the end if he keeps asking. So, he said, “⟦Q 144:2.3⟧Ask and it shall be given you; seek and you shall find; knock and it shall be opened to you⟦/Q⟧”. Even an earthly father gives good things, not harmful ones, to a child who asks foolishly, and the heavenly Father does so all the more.
p144.008: He also told the story of a widow who kept going back to an unjust judge. But Jesus explained that persistent prayer does not change God's mind; it changes our attitude and enlarges our capacity to receive the spirit of God.
p144.010: When James asked again for a prayer for the new believers, Jesus gave them the prayer he had taught his brothers and sisters in Nazareth. It begins with “⟦Q 144:3.3⟧Our Father who is in heaven⟦/Q⟧”, asks that the Father's will be done on earth too, asks him to forgive us as we have forgiven, and ends with “⟦Q 144:3.12⟧And increasingly make us perfect like yourself⟦/Q⟧”. The Urantia Book explains that this is the prayer known today as the Lord's Prayer, and that in later times two lines were dropped and another phrase was added.
p144.011: Jesus did not like to pray in front of others, and he told the apostles to pray alone in a quiet place too. A good prayer is unselfish, full of faith, sincere, intelligent, and trusting in the Father's will. When Jesus prayed all night, he prayed more for his followers than for himself.
p144.013: Jesus taught them more about prayer. A sincere prayer offered in faith, even if it asks for something foolish, enlarges the soul's capacity. Becoming a child of God is not something we earn by hard effort; it is a gift we receive by grace.
p144.014: The Urantia Book says that prayer is a remedy that guards against harmful self-examination, and that it is like recharging the soul's spiritual batteries. Worship is compared to tuning the soul in to the broadcasts God sends out. Prayer is the process of changing the person I am now into the person I ought to become. Jesus prayed mostly in silence, within his heart.
p144.016: Jesus shared several more prayers to use as examples when explaining other matters. These were prayers from other worlds, but he told them not to teach them to the public. The Urantia Book includes seven of them. These prayers ask that the Father live within us and make us more and more like him, and that he take us by the hand and lead us step by step along the uncertain path of life. Most of them end with the words “⟦Q 144:5.50⟧not our will but yours be done⟦/Q⟧”. The apostles did not teach these prayers in public, but they drew great help from them in their personal spiritual lives.
p144.018: At the beginning of October, the apostles met John's apostles in a marketplace. John had recently set apart twelve men as apostles too, and their leader was Abner. The twenty-four men of the two groups held a conference at the Gilboa camp for three weeks. Jesus spoke only three times, about sympathy, cooperation, and tolerance, and did not take part in the discussions. He said that he helped with individuals' spiritual problems, but that they must make the rules of their group themselves, and he went away for two weeks.
p144.019: The twenty-four agreed to use together the prayer Jesus had taught them. The hardest question was baptism. They decided that while John was alive, John's apostles would baptize and Jesus' apostles would teach. Even when they disagreed, they learned to respect one another's views by discussing, praying, and giving way to each other. When Jesus returned, he said he would gladly support their decisions.
p144.021: In November and December, Jesus and the twenty-four worked quietly in the Greek cities of the Decapolis. One of Jesus' apostles and one of John's apostles went out as a pair; one baptized and the other taught. The Urantia Book says that whenever a new religion tries to take in the people of an older one, it always ends up giving something up, and this time the price was water baptism. At first John's apostles believed in Jesus because of John's testimony, but soon they came to believe through knowing Jesus for themselves. Abner later became the leader of the seventy gospel teachers.
p144.023: At the end of December, while the group was teaching near Pella, John sent his disciples from prison to ask, “⟦Q 144:8.2⟧are you truly the Deliverer, or shall we look for another?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus told them to let John know that he had not been forgotten and that the gospel was being preached to the poor. And he said that John was not a reed shaken by the wind, but a man greater than a prophet. Yet in the kingdom of heaven, he said, even the least person is greater than John, because he knows that he is a child of God.
p144.024: From that day on the two groups of apostles were firmly united as one. Jesus compared people who would accept neither John nor himself to children grumbling in the marketplace. And he invited everyone: “⟦Q 144:8.8⟧Come, therefore, all you who labor and are heavy laden⟦/Q⟧”, and find rest.
p144.026: On January 10, A.D. 28, John the Baptist was executed by Herod's order. When John's disciples brought the news, Jesus said that the time had now come to proclaim the kingdom openly and powerfully. The next morning Jesus and the apostles left for Galilee. This paper teaches us that prayer is not a magic spell that changes God, but a breath that enlarges our hearts. It also shows that people who think differently can respect one another and work together.
p145.002: After John the Baptist died, Jesus and the apostles returned to Capernaum in January of A.D. 28. Jesus was getting ready for his first public preaching tour of Galilee, and for a few days he taught the apostles and met with the people who came to see him. On Friday night his youngest sister, Ruth, came secretly to visit him, and they spent an hour together on a boat. The Urantia Book says that Ruth was the only one in the family who believed in her brother's mission from beginning to end and never once wavered.
p145.004: On Friday morning, so many people crowded around that Jesus got into a boat and taught for more than two hours. The boat belonged to fishermen who had worked all night and caught nothing. When he finished teaching, Jesus told them to let down their nets in the deep water, and they caught so many fish that the nets nearly broke. A fisherman named Simon fell down before Jesus and said, “⟦Q 145:1.2⟧I am a sinful man⟦/Q⟧”, and from that day on they followed Jesus.
p145.005: But The Urantia Book explains that this was not a miracle. Jesus was an experienced fisherman who watched nature closely, and he simply knew where the schools of fish would be at that hour. Even so, people always thought of it as a miracle.
p145.007: On the Sabbath afternoon, Jesus preached in the synagogue on “⟦Q 145:2.1⟧The Will of the Father in Heaven⟦/Q⟧”. He said that people should come to the Father not as children of Israel but each one as a child of God. Until then religion had been the religion of a nation; now it would be a personal religion, in which each person knows God directly. He added that Jeremiah and Ezekiel had already looked ahead to the day when God would write his law in people's hearts and give them a new spirit.
p145.008: Jesus said that God does not punish a whole nation for the sin of one person, and he does not punish one believing child for the sins of a nation. The hope of a better nation and a better world depends on each person growing and waking up. Hearing this sermon, the apostles understood more clearly that the gospel of the kingdom is a message to the individual, not to the nation. The people were amazed that Jesus taught with authority, unlike the scribes.
p145.009: When the sermon ended, a young man had a seizure and cried out, and Jesus took him by the hand and said, “⟦Q 145:2.12⟧Come out of it⟦/Q⟧”. The Urantia Book explains that he was not possessed by an evil spirit; he had epilepsy. Yet people spread the story that Jesus had cast out a demon. When the fever of Peter's mother-in-law happened to break while Jesus was beside her, that too spread as a miracle. The Urantia Book says that people who loved miracles counted even such coincidences as miracles.
p145.011: At sundown, when the Sabbath ended, nearly a thousand sick people who had heard the news crowded into the front yard of Zebedee's house. That day Jesus had spoken these words: “⟦Q 145:3.4⟧Hate is the shadow of fear; revenge the mask of cowardice⟦/Q⟧”. Jesus knew that a spiritual movement could not be built on miracles, so until then he had not used his supernatural power. But when he saw the suffering people, his heart was deeply moved. That day's sermon had gone straight to people's consciences and souls. They also could not forget his words, “⟦Q 145:3.4⟧Man is the son of God, not a child of the devil⟦/Q⟧”. As the sun went down, the sick and their families filled the roads leading into Capernaum, and someone among them cried out, “⟦Q 145:3.8⟧Master, speak the word⟦/Q⟧”!
p145.012: Jesus said that he wished them to be made whole if it was not against his Father's will. Because the Father's will did not oppose it, in that moment 683 people were healed of all their diseases. Nothing like this had happened before, and nothing like it happened afterward. The one most surprised by it was Jesus himself. The Urantia Book explains that what a Creator Son desires and the Father wills simply comes to pass at once.
p145.013: Because of this, Jesus' name spread through the whole region, and Herod became afraid again. From then on Jesus was known as a healer as much as a preacher. But most of the people who were healed did not change much spiritually. These so-called miracles brought him fame he did not want, and in the end they caused Jesus a great deal of trouble.
p145.015: That night the apostles were overjoyed. They believed the kingdom was finally beginning to come with power. But Jesus was nowhere to be found. When he came back late, he refused their congratulations and said only this: “⟦Q 145:4.2⟧Rejoice not that my Father is powerful to heal the body, but rather that he is mighty to save the soul.⟦/Q⟧” The apostles went to bed disappointed and confused.
p145.017: Jesus, too, hardly slept that night. He was worried that healing bodies would take up all his time, and that building the spiritual kingdom in people's hearts would be pushed aside. Early in the morning he went out alone to pray, and the apostles came looking for him. Andrew told him that everyone was looking for him and urged him to come back.
p145.018: When Peter, James, and John found Jesus at dawn, he spent more than four hours explaining why the Father's kingdom could not be built on miracles and physical healing. But the apostles did not really understand what he meant. The Urantia Book also tells us that Jesus often went up into the hills to pray because he had no room where he could be quietly alone.
p145.019: Jesus said that the people were coming not to seek the truth but to have their bodies healed. Caring for the sick is important, he said, but they must not get so caught up in healing that they lose the teaching. Then he said they should leave right away for the other towns of Galilee. The apostles were sorry to go, but Thomas said: “⟦Q 145:5.10⟧We follow a teacher who seeks no glory for himself.⟦/Q⟧” A heart made new is more precious than any amazing thing we can see with our eyes. That is the lesson this paper gives us.
p146.002: For two months starting in January of A.D. 28, Jesus and the twelve apostles, together with John's former apostles, traveled through the towns of Galilee preaching the gospel. It was the first tour on which Jesus let the apostles preach without any limits. He only asked them to avoid Nazareth and to be careful in Capernaum and Tiberias. The apostles gladly preached the gospel, cared for the sick, and baptized those who believed.
p146.004: Rimmon was a city that had long ago been dedicated to a Babylonian god of the air. The people there still held many of the old beliefs of Babylon and Persia, so Jesus and the apostles spent a lot of time explaining how those beliefs differed from the new gospel. The Urantia Book says that it is hard for people who once worshiped nature to fully accept spiritual ideals within a single lifetime. It also explains that good ideas from the East about light and darkness and good and evil, along with the thought of Plato, later found their way into Christian teaching, and this helped people in many places accept the gospel more easily.
p146.006: At Jotapata, when Nathaniel asked about prayer, Jesus taught about it in detail. If we stubbornly hold on to wrongdoing in our hearts, our fellowship with God slowly breaks off. God forgives us even before we ask, but we truly experience that forgiveness only when we forgive others. No matter how great love is, salvation cannot be forced on someone who does not choose for himself to live forever.
p146.007: Jesus said that prayer does not change God's mind; it changes our attitude toward God. Prayer is not a way to get ahead of others or to lift ourselves up. He told them to pray less for themselves alone and more for the spiritual growth of others. Praying for sick people cannot take the place of actually caring for them. We should know how to talk to the Father not only when we are in trouble but also when all is well.
p146.008: Jesus was also sorry that there was so little thanksgiving in our prayers. After praying, he said, we should wait quietly for a while and give the spirit within us a chance to speak. And he taught that worship is an experience that makes us more and more like the one we worship. The one phrase that fits every prayer is “⟦Q 146:2.12⟧Nevertheless, your will be done⟦/Q⟧”.
p146.010: At Ramah, Jesus patiently listened to an old Greek philosopher who believed that science and philosophy were enough, and he agreed with the points that were true. Then he said that something was missing: the answers to where we came from, why we are here, and where we are going. After talking for more than an hour, the philosopher believed the gospel. When the apostles were surprised, Jesus said that “⟦Q 146:3.2⟧intolerance is the mask covering up the entertainment of secret doubts as to the trueness of one's belief⟦/Q⟧”. True certainty is not afraid of honest criticism.
p146.011: When Thomas asked how a new believer could be sure the gospel is true, Jesus said that this certainty comes from personal experience. And he said there is a practical way to know how much we have given ourselves over to the spirit of God: by how much we love our neighbors. He also promised that soon the Spirit of Truth would be poured out on all people and would tell us that we are children of God.
p146.013: In the mining town of Iron, Jesus wanted to understand the miners' lives, so he worked with them down in the mines. One day a man with leprosy knelt before him and said that if the Lord was willing, he could make him clean. The man believed he could not enter the kingdom unless he was healed. Jesus was moved, and he touched him and said, “⟦Q 146:4.3⟧I will—be clean⟦/Q⟧”, and the man was healed at once. The Urantia Book says this was the first so-called miracle that Jesus did on purpose.
p146.014: Jesus told him not to tell anyone, but the man spread the news all over town. So many sick people crowded in that Jesus had to leave. Afterward, in Chorazin and Madon, very few people believed. The apostles hoped Jesus would show them more amazing works, but he did not give in.
p146.016: While Jesus was staying in Cana, Titus, a nobleman from Capernaum, came and begged him to heal his dying son. Jesus was sad that people would not believe unless they saw signs, and then he said, “⟦Q 146:5.2⟧Return to your home; your son will live.⟦/Q⟧” The boy's fever broke at that very hour, and the whole family came to believe. The Urantia Book explains that this was not a miracle of healing; it was a case in which Jesus knew ahead of time what nature would do. Still, when the news spread, Jesus again had to leave in a hurry.
p146.018: By this time the people expected nothing but miracles from Jesus. In front of the gate of Nain, the group met the funeral procession of a widow's only son. When people begged him to bring the son back to life, Jesus examined the boy and saw that he was not really dead. Jesus said, “⟦Q 146:6.2⟧Awake and arise⟦/Q⟧”, and the boy got up.
p146.019: Jesus explained again and again that the boy had not died but had been in a deep sleep, but no one believed him. People thought Jesus was hiding his miracle out of humility, and the story that he had raised the dead spread through the whole region. Early the next day Jesus left for Endor.
p146.021: At Endor, Jesus rested for a few days away from the crowds. He told them the story of King Saul and the witch of Endor and explained that the souls of the dead do not come back to talk with the living. What people thought were the spirits of the dead were really rebel spirit beings, and he said they would soon no longer be able to trouble people.
p146.022: This paper shows that chasing after wonders is different from true faith. How close we are to God is shown not by whether we have seen a miracle but by how much we love our neighbors.
p147.002: After the tour of Galilee, Jesus and the apostles returned to Capernaum in the middle of March and stayed for two weeks. Jesus even went secretly to Tiberias to teach the believers in Herod's household. They explained to Herod that Jesus' kingdom was spiritual, not political, and Herod's hostility softened. The greatest danger to Jesus was not Herod but the religious leaders in Jerusalem. That is why Jesus taught mostly in Galilee.
p147.004: The day before they left for Jerusalem, Mangus, a Roman centurion in Capernaum, sent Jewish elders to ask Jesus to heal his dying servant. He loved the Jewish people so much that he had even built them a synagogue. As Jesus was going to his house, the centurion sent friends to tell him this: he was not worthy to have the Lord come into his house, and he believed that if Jesus would only speak the word from where he was, his servant would be healed.
p147.005: Jesus was amazed and said, “⟦Q 147:1.3⟧I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel⟦/Q⟧”, and he turned back. From that hour the servant began to get better. The Urantia Book honestly says that we do not know whether unseen beings did the healing at that time; we only know that the servant fully recovered.
p147.007: At the end of March, Jesus and the apostles set out for Jerusalem to keep the Passover, and they stayed at Bethany. On the way, Judas deposited part of their common fund in a bank at Jericho. Crowds looking for healing and comfort came to Bethany too, so Jesus went back and forth between Gethsemane and Bethany. This time he had them teach only personally, with no public preaching. In Bethany, Jesus and the twelve quietly kept their first Passover without blood. John's apostles stayed in Jerusalem working with Abner, and the two groups kept on good terms with each other.
p147.009: One Sabbath, John took Jesus to the pool of Bethesda. The pool was a hot spring that bubbled up from time to time, and people believed that whoever got into the water first when it moved would be healed. John hoped that if Jesus saw the sick people and worked a miracle, all Jerusalem would believe. Jesus asked John not to try to turn him from the path he had chosen, but he still gathered the sick people and spoke words of comfort to them.
p147.010: Jesus told them that they were all children of God and that God loved them. Being freed from bodily illness is wonderful, he said, but being healed from spiritual sickness and moral weakness is an even greater thing. Hearing these words, a man who had lain helpless for a long time joyfully picked up his bed and walked away. He had only waited for someone to help him and had never thought of getting up on his own. Yet getting up by himself was the one thing he needed to do to be healed.
p147.012: That evening Nathaniel asked a question. What if a person with evil intentions misused the rule that says to treat others the way you want to be treated? Jesus explained six levels of understanding this rule. There is the level of the flesh, which thinks only of one's own wants; the level of the feelings, which adds sympathy and pity; the level of the mind, which adds sound judgment and self-respect; the level of brotherly love, which is devoted to the welfare of one's neighbors; and the moral level, which sees right and wrong through the eyes of a fair third party.
p147.013: And at the highest, spiritual level, the rule means to treat people the way God would treat them. Jesus said, “⟦Q 147:4.9⟧I would, therefore, that you should do to all men that which you know I would do to them in like circumstances⟦/Q⟧”. The apostles were greatly amazed by these words and talked about them for a long time.
p147.015: Simon, a Pharisee, invited Jesus to dinner. While they were there, a woman whom people pointed at as a sinner came in. She had believed the gospel and given up her old life, but people still looked down on her. The woman wet Jesus' feet with her tears, wiped them with her hair, and anointed them with ointment. Simon thought to himself that if Jesus were a prophet, he would have known what kind of woman this was.
p147.016: Jesus asked which of two people would love more, one forgiven a large debt or one forgiven a small one. Then he said that this woman, who had been forgiven much, loved that much, and he told her, “⟦Q 147:5.5⟧Woman, go in peace; your faith has saved you.⟦/Q⟧” He also said that no one can shut the door of the kingdom of heaven in the face of someone who wants to come in by faith.
p147.017: That evening Jesus taught that what matters is not where you are now but which direction you are going. “⟦Q 147:5.7⟧What you are becoming day by day is of infinitely more importance than what you are today.⟦/Q⟧” A small but living, growing faith is better than great knowledge. But Jesus also warned clearly that God is not a soft parent who overlooks everything.
p147.019: At the end of April the group went back to Capernaum. Meanwhile, the leaders in Jerusalem decided to put Jesus on trial on religious charges, and they sent six spies to follow him. On a Sabbath, when the hungry apostles rubbed grain in their hands and ate it as they walked through the wheat fields, the spies accused them of breaking the Sabbath law.
p147.020: Jesus gave the example of David, who when hungry ate the bread that only the priests were allowed to eat, and he said it was better to look after people's health and well-being than to keep the Sabbath. And he declared “⟦Q 147:6.4⟧that the Sabbath was made for man and not man for the Sabbath⟦/Q⟧”. Rather than condemn the old traditions, Jesus showed the true way in a positive way.
p147.022: In Capernaum, when the leader of the spies asked why Jesus did not make his disciples fast, Jesus answered that people do not fast while the bridegroom is with them. Just as no one sews a piece of new cloth onto an old garment, and new wine is put into new wineskins, they should not bring too much of the old order into the gospel. At the same time, he said, they should keep what is true even if it is old, throw away what is false even if it is new, and bravely accept what is new and true.
p147.024: That night Jesus quoted the words of Isaiah as he taught the apostles. The fast that pleases God is not making the body suffer. It is setting the oppressed free, sharing bread with the hungry, and welcoming the homeless. When we do this, our light will shine in the darkness like the morning.
p147.025: Jesus taught that it is faith, not making the body suffer, that keeps us safe in the kingdom of heaven. His last words that night were these: “⟦Q 147:8.5⟧Grow in grace by means of that living faith which grasps the fact that you are the sons of God while at the same time it recognizes every man as a brother.⟦/Q⟧” Even if we fall a little short today, if we are moving step by step toward God, that is what matters most.
